scope: 13 targeted original AQA AS Waves 3.3.1.2/3.3.1.3/3.3.2.2 cards on aerial polarisation, node-loop phase, harmonics and qualitative slit diffraction
notes: AQA does not require Malus's law, the historical term fundamental or the terms overtone. These cards use first/third harmonic terminology and do not require laser operation.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For receiving a linearly polarised radio signal, when is a straight receiving aerial best aligned?
accept: Parallel to the electric-field oscillations.
parallel to the wave's polarisation direction
Align the aerial length with the direction of the incident E-field.
reject: parallel to the direction of wave travel
The receiving aerial must be perpendicular to the electric oscillation direction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What happens to ideal linearly polarised light passing through a second polariser at 90° to the first?
accept: No light is transmitted.
zero transmission
Crossed ideal polarisers block the transmitted light completely.
reject: Two ideal polarisers crossed at 90 degrees transmit all the light.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does the polarisation of light provide evidence that it is transverse?
cards.back: Only transverse oscillations can be restricted to a chosen vibration plane.
accept: Only transverse oscillations can be restricted to a chosen vibration plane.
only transverse waves can be polarised
Polarisation selects a vibration plane, possible only for transverse waves.
reject: light must be a mechanical wave
Longitudinal pressure waves can be linearly polarised in the same way.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How does displacement change at a node of an ideal stationary wave over time?
accept: It remains zero.
the node stays at zero displacement
A node is permanently at zero displacement.
reject: the node travels along the string
A node alternates between positive and negative maximum displacement.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do points in the same loop between adjacent nodes oscillate in a stationary string wave?
accept: In phase.
same phase
Particles in a single loop have zero phase difference.
reject: Points within the same loop are in antiphase.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do points in adjacent loops of an ideal stationary string wave oscillate?
accept: In antiphase (180° apart).
180 degrees out of phase
Neighbouring loops have a phase difference of pi radians.
reject: Adjacent loops of a stationary wave move in phase.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How many antinodes occur on a fixed-end string in its third harmonic?
accept: Three.
Third harmonic has 3 antinodes.
reject: The third harmonic has two antinodes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How many nodes, including the ends, occur on a fixed-end string in its third harmonic?
accept: Four.
There are four fixed nodes including both ends.
reject: A third-harmonic fixed string has only three nodes including its ends.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Fixed L and μ: string tension rises ninefold. How does first-harmonic frequency change?
cards.back: It becomes three times as large.
accept: It becomes three times as large.
frequency triples
Since f is proportional to the square root of tension, it triples.
reject: frequency becomes nine times as large
Increasing tension ninefold increases frequency ninefold.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In an experiment with fixed L and μ, why is f² plotted against string tension T?
cards.back: The relationship f²=T/(4L²μ) is a straight line through the origin.
accept: The relationship f²=T/(4L²μ) is a straight line through the origin.
frequency squared is proportional to tension
Squaring f gives a linear relation with T at constant L and mu.
reject: frequency is inversely proportional to tension
f squared is independent of tension
Plotting f squared against T gives a quadratic curve.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For single-slit diffraction at fixed wavelength, what happens to the central maximum if slit width decreases?
accept: The central maximum becomes wider.
central diffraction peak broadens
A narrower slit causes greater spreading, widening the central fringe.
reject: Decreasing slit width narrows the central bright maximum.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In the qualitative single-slit pattern, how does the central bright maximum compare in width with the side maxima?
accept: The central maximum is wider.
centre bright fringe is the widest
The central bright fringe is broader than an individual side fringe.
reject: All bright maxima are the same width in single-slit diffraction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: In the qualitative single-slit diffraction pattern for white light, what colour is the central bright maximum?
accept: White.
white central maximum
